title: Vanishing gradient for generator early in training
description: Early in learning, when G is poor, D can reject samples with high confidence because they are clearly different from the training data. In this case, log(1-D(G(z))) saturates and provides insufficient gradient for G to learn well.

verdict.reasoning: Papers 1 and 2 (the LSGAN paper and its effectiveness analysis) directly identify the gap's exact mechanism — the sigmoid cross-entropy loss causing log(1-D(G(z))) to saturate when the discriminator confidently rejects poor samples — and propose a concrete, theoretically grounded fix: replacing sigmoid cross-entropy with a least-squares loss that penalizes distance to the decision boundary, thereby providing non-zero gradients even for correctly-classified but distant fake samples. Both demonstrate empirically that this resolves the vanishing-gradient issue and stabilizes training. Papers 3 and 4 offer partial insight but either sidestep the original formulation (Kernel GANs) or show limited empirical success for the exact saturating loss (α-GANs). Paper 5 addresses a different gradient-noise problem, not the saturation mechanism. Since Paper 1 alone is a direct_solution that fully addresses the gap, the gap is convincingly solved.

paper.title: Least Squares Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: Unsupervised learning with generative adversarial networks (GANs) has proven hugely successful. Regular GANs hypothesize the discriminator as a classifier with the sigmoid cross entropy loss function. However, we found that this loss function may lead to the vanishing gradients problem during the learning process. To overcome such a problem, we propose in this paper the Least Squares Generative Adversarial Networks (LSGANs) which adopt the least squares loss function for the discriminator. We show that minimizing the objective function of LSGAN yields minimizing the Pearson $χ^2$ divergence. There are two benefits of LSGANs over regular GANs. First, LSGANs are able to generate higher quality images than regular GANs. Second, LSGANs perform more stable during the learning process. We evaluate LSGANs on five scene datasets and the experimental results show that the images generated by LSGANs are of better quality than the ones generated by regular GANs. We also conduct two comparison experiments between LSGANs and regular GANs to illustrate the stability of LSGANs.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper directly addresses the vanishing gradient problem for the generator early in GAN training. It identifies that the sigmoid cross-entropy loss used in regular GANs causes vanishing gradients when the discriminator confidently rejects poor samples (i.e., samples on the correct side of the decision boundary but far from real data produce almost no error signal). The paper proposes replacing the sigmoid cross-entropy loss with a least squares loss, which penalizes samples based on their distance to the decision boundary, thereby providing non-vanishing gradients even when samples are correctly classified. The paper provides theoretical analysis showing LSGANs minimize Pearson χ² divergence, and demonstrates empirically that LSGANs are more stable and less prone to mode collapse than regular GANs, including in ablation studies without batch normalization.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper fully addresses the specific gap of vanishing gradients for the generator early in training caused by discriminator overconfidence. It identifies the problem, proposes a solution (least squares loss), provides theoretical grounding, and demonstrates empirically that the solution mitigates the issue. No part of this specific gap remains unaddressed.
evidence_snippets: Regular GANs adopt the sigmoid cross entropy loss function for the discriminator. We argue that this loss function, however, will lead to the problem of vanishing gradients when updating the generator using the fake samples that are on the correct side of the decision boundary, but are still far from the real data.

When we use the fake samples (in magenta) to update the generator by making the discriminator believe they are from real data, it will cause almost no error because they are on the correct side, i.e., the real data side, of the decision boundary.

Penalizing the samples lying a long way to the decision boundary can generate more gradients when updating the generator, which in turn relieves the problem of vanishing gradients. This allows LSGANs to perform more stable during the learning process.

paper.title: On the Effectiveness of Least Squares Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: Unsupervised learning with generative adversarial networks (GANs) has proven to be hugely successful. Regular GANs hypothesize the discriminator as a classifier with the sigmoid cross entropy loss function. However, we found that this loss function may lead to the vanishing gradients problem during the learning process. To overcome such a problem, we propose in this paper the Least Squares Generative Adversarial Networks (LSGANs) which adopt the least squares loss for both the discriminator and the generator. We show that minimizing the objective function of LSGAN yields minimizing the Pearson $χ^2$ divergence. We also show that the derived objective function that yields minimizing the Pearson $χ^2$ divergence performs better than the classical one of using least squares for classification. There are two benefits of LSGANs over regular GANs. First, LSGANs are able to generate higher quality images than regular GANs. Second, LSGANs perform more stably during the learning process. For evaluating the image quality, we conduct both qualitative and quantitative experiments, and the experimental results show that LSGANs can generate higher quality images than regular GANs. Furthermore, we evaluate the stability of LSGANs in two groups. One is to compare between LSGANs and regular GANs without gradient penalty. We conduct three experiments, including Gaussian mixture distribution, difficult architectures, and a newly proposed method --- datasets with small variability, to illustrate the stability of LSGANs. The other one is to compare between LSGANs with gradient penalty (LSGANs-GP) and WGANs with gradient penalty (WGANs-GP). The experimental results show that LSGANs-GP succeed in training for all the difficult architectures used in WGANs-GP, including 101-layer ResNet.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper directly addresses the vanishing gradient problem for the generator early in GAN training. It identifies that both the minimax loss (log(1-D(G(z)))) and the non-saturating loss (-log(D(G(z)))) saturate when the discriminator confidently rejects poor samples, providing insufficient gradients. The paper proposes Least Squares GANs (LSGANs) which replace the sigmoid cross-entropy loss with a least squares loss. The key insight is that the least squares loss penalizes samples based on their distance to the decision boundary, so even correctly-classified fake samples that are far from real data still receive gradients to pull them toward the decision boundary. The paper provides theoretical analysis showing LSGANs minimize Pearson χ² divergence, and demonstrates through experiments that LSGANs alleviate the vanishing gradient problem and improve training stability.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper fully addresses the specific gap of vanishing gradients for the generator early in training when the discriminator confidently rejects poor samples. It identifies the problem, proposes a solution (least squares loss), provides theoretical justification, and empirically demonstrates that LSGANs provide better gradients in this regime. No part of this specific gap remains unaddressed.

paper.title: Non-parametric estimation of Jensen-Shannon Divergence in Generative Adversarial Network training
paper.abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have become a widely popular framework for generative modelling of high-dimensional datasets. However their training is well-known to be difficult. This work presents a rigorous statistical analysis of GANs providing straight-forward explanations for common training pathologies such as vanishing gradients. Furthermore, it proposes a new training objective, Kernel GANs, and demonstrates its practical effectiveness on large-scale real-world data sets. A key element in the analysis is the distinction between training with respect to the (unknown) data distribution, and its empirical counterpart. To overcome issues in GAN training, we pursue the idea of smoothing the Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) by incorporating noise in the input distributions of the discriminator. As we show, this effectively leads to an empirical version of the JSD in which the true and the generator densities are replaced by kernel density estimates, which leads to Kernel GANs.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper provides a rigorous mathematical analysis showing that vanishing gradients in GAN training arise from the discrete nature of the empirical training objective, where the supports of empirical distributions are disjoint, making it trivial for the discriminator to separate real from generated samples. To address this, the paper proposes Kernel GANs, which smooth the Jensen-Shannon Divergence by adding noise to input distributions, leading to kernel density estimates that prevent the discriminator from saturating. The discriminator is unrolled to closed-form optimality, avoiding the vanishing gradient problem that occurs when the discriminator becomes too confident.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper's solution (Kernel GANs) changes the training paradigm significantly by replacing the adversarial discriminator with an implicit one based on kernel density estimates, rather than fixing the original GAN training dynamics. The paper acknowledges that even with smoothing, the optimal generator still only guarantees reproducing training samples (not generalization). The approach requires careful bandwidth selection and the regularizer φ introduces asymptotic bias. The solution does not address the specific issue of log(1-D(G(z))) saturation in the original GAN formulation — it sidesteps it by reformulating the objective entirely. Additionally, the paper does not fully resolve the practical challenge of balancing generator and discriminator training in the original adversarial setup.
evidence_snippets: This yields a straight-forward explanation for common pathologies in practical GAN training such as vanishing gradients.
To overcome such issues, we pursue the idea of smoothing the Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) by incorporating noise in the input distributions of the discriminator.
This suggests the primary reason for vanishing gradients in GAN training is the discrete nature of the empirical objective ([REF:eq:empirical_objective]) -- which is a remarkably simple explanation.

paper.title: Addressing GAN Training Instabilities via Tunable Classification Losses
paper.abstract: Generative adversarial networks (GANs), modeled as a zero-sum game between a generator (G) and a discriminator (D), allow generating synthetic data with formal guarantees. Noting that D is a classifier, we begin by reformulating the GAN value function using class probability estimation (CPE) losses. We prove a two-way correspondence between CPE loss GANs and $f$-GANs which minimize $f$-divergences. We also show that all symmetric $f$-divergences are equivalent in convergence. In the finite sample and model capacity setting, we define and obtain bounds on estimation and generalization errors. We specialize these results to $α$-GANs, defined using $α$-loss, a tunable CPE loss family parametrized by $α\in(0,\infty]$. We next introduce a class of dual-objective GANs to address training instabilities of GANs by modeling each player's objective using $α$-loss to obtain $(α_D,α_G)$-GANs. We show that the resulting non-zero sum game simplifies to minimizing an $f$-divergence under appropriate conditions on $(α_D,α_G)$. Generalizing this dual-objective formulation using CPE losses, we define and obtain upper bounds on an appropriately defined estimation error. Finally, we highlight the value of tuning $(α_D,α_G)$ in alleviating training instabilities for the synthetic 2D Gaussian mixture ring as well as the large publicly available Celeb-A and LSUN Classroom image datasets.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper explicitly identifies the vanishing gradient problem for the generator early in training (when D confidently rejects poor samples, causing log(1-D(G(z))) to saturate). It proposes $(\alpha_D,\alpha_G)$-GANs, a tunable dual-objective framework using $\alpha$-loss, and provides a theoretical gradient analysis showing how the gradient magnitude scalar $C_{x,\alpha_D,\alpha_G} = \alpha_D D_{\omega^*}(x)(1-D_{\omega^*}(x))^{1-1/\alpha_G}$ can be modulated by tuning $\alpha_D$ and $\alpha_G$. For the saturating generator loss (the exact formulation in the gap), the analysis shows that the gradient magnitude depends on these parameters, offering a mechanism to mitigate vanishing gradients.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper's own experimental results on the 2D ring dataset for the saturating (exact gap) setting show that tuning $\alpha_G$ (the generator's parameter) away from 1 has "no significant impact on GAN performance" — it is tuning $\alpha_D$ below 1 that helps. This means the direct solution to the gap (preventing saturation of the generator's gradient when D is confident) via the generator's own loss parameter is empirically limited. The non-saturating formulation (which changes the objective to $-\log D(G(z))$ rather than fixing the saturating $\log(1-D(G(z)))$) works better, but that is a different objective than the one the gap describes. The paper does not provide a complete resolution of the saturating gradient problem for the original $\log(1-D(G(z)))$ formulation; it provides partial theoretical insight and partial empirical mitigation via discriminator-side tuning.
evidence_snippets: Goodfellow et al. note that the generator's objective in the vanilla GAN can saturate early in training (due to the use of the sigmoid activation) when D can easily distinguish between the real and synthetic samples, i.e., when the output of D is near zero for all synthetic samples, leading to vanishing gradients.

Compared to the vanilla GAN performance, we find that tuning $\alpha_{D}$ below 1 leads to a greater success rate and lower failure rate. However, in this saturating loss setting, we find that tuning $\alpha_{G}$ away from 1 has no significant impact on GAN performance.

paper.title: Adversarial symmetric GANs: bridging adversarial samples and adversarial networks
paper.abstract: Generative adversarial networks have achieved remarkable performance on various tasks but suffer from training instability. Despite many training strategies proposed to improve training stability, this issue remains as a challenge. In this paper, we investigate the training instability from the perspective of adversarial samples and reveal that adversarial training on fake samples is implemented in vanilla GANs, but adversarial training on real samples has long been overlooked. Consequently, the discriminator is extremely vulnerable to adversarial perturbation and the gradient given by the discriminator contains non-informative adversarial noises, which hinders the generator from catching the pattern of real samples. Here, we develop adversarial symmetric GANs (AS-GANs) that incorporate adversarial training of the discriminator on real samples into vanilla GANs, making adversarial training symmetrical. The discriminator is therefore more robust and provides more informative gradient with less adversarial noise, thereby stabilizing training and accelerating convergence. The effectiveness of the AS-GANs is verified on image generation on CIFAR-10 , CelebA, and LSUN with varied network architectures. Not only the training is more stabilized, but the FID scores of generated samples are consistently improved by a large margin compared to the baseline. The bridging of adversarial samples and adversarial networks provides a new approach to further develop adversarial networks.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes AS-GANs, which add adversarial training on real samples (using FGSM perturbations) to make the discriminator more robust and reduce "adversarial noise" in the gradients passed to the generator. The authors show that this produces gradients with more semantic information and less noise, leading to more stable training, faster convergence, and better FID scores on several image datasets. The method is related to the gap because it addresses gradient quality issues in GAN training, which includes the early-training period.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not specifically address the mechanism described in the gap: the saturation of log(1-D(G(z))) when the discriminator confidently rejects poor samples early in training. The paper's solution (adversarial training on real samples) addresses a different problem — reducing adversarial noise in the discriminator's gradients — rather than preventing the discriminator from saturating when G is poor. The early-training saturation problem (where gradients vanish because D's output is near 0 for all generated samples) is not explicitly tackled; the paper does not modify the loss function, add gradient penalties near generated samples, or otherwise prevent the discriminator from becoming too confident early on. The gap's specific issue of insufficient gradient signal when G is poor remains open.
evidence_snippets: We find that this is partly because adversarial training on real samples, or training the discriminator with adversarial samples of real data, has been neglected, which results in the gradient of the discriminator still containing considerable adversarial noises.

the gradient given by the discriminator that guides update of the generator is exactly the same as the gradient used to craft adversarial samples of the discriminator.
